title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 8–10 (Night 223, continuing nights-222), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 223 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The treasurer chases his bolting horse into a wood, where a huge and hideous lion comes at him; unarmed, he blames his plight on the wrong he was sent to do the two princes. Meanwhile al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, left bound and parched with thirst, wish they had been killed; al-Asʿad works his bonds loose, frees his brother and takes up the emir's sword, and the two follow the tracks into the wood together. They find the lion on top of the treasurer, and al-Amjad kills it with a blow between the eyes; the treasurer throws himself at their feet and vows to ransom them with his own life, and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-third night,
sentences.n: As at every night's opening: the unit, al-thālithatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, and both stand in the nominative with al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْخَازِنْدَارَ لَمَّا ذَهَبَ وَرَاءَ فَرَسِهِ وَقَدِ الْتَهَبَ فُؤَادُهُ وَمَا زَالَ يَجْرِي خَلْفَهُ لِيُمْسِكَهُ حَتَّى دَخَلَ فِي غَابَةٍ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-khāzindāra lammā dhahaba warāʾa farasihi wa-qadi iltahaba fuʾāduhu wa-mā zāla yajrī khalfahu li-yumsikahu ḥattā dakhala fī ghābatin
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-treasurer, when he-went behind his-horse — and-had blazed-up his-heart — and-not ceased he-runs after-it to-catch-it, until it-entered into a-wood.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the treasurer went after his horse, his heart on fire, he kept running after it to catch it, until it ran into a wood.
sentences.n: The print has فؤادة, a misprint for فؤاده, corrected here. Shahrazād takes up the last words of the night before. As there, the print runs al-saʿīdu and anna together as one word, السعيدان; it is kept as set and read as the two words al-saʿīdu anna, “fortunate, that”; anna takes its noun, al-khāzindāra, in the accusative. The lammā clause, “when he went after his horse”, finds its answer only in fa-dakhala warāʾahu, “he went in after it”, at the head of the next sentence; the fa- before the answer is the storyteller's usage. wa-qadi iltahaba fuʾāduhu, “his heart having blazed up”: wa- with qad and the perfect makes a circumstantial clause; iltahaba, Form VIII of l-h-b, “to flare up”, of anger and alarm; qad takes a kasra before the joined alif. mā zāla with an imperfect, “he kept on running”. li-yumsikahu: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, “in order to catch it”. The ء of وراء and the ؤ of فؤاده are printed.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ وَرَاءَهُ فِي تِلْكَ الْغَابَةِ فَشَقَّ الْجَوَادُ فِي وَسَطِ الْغَابَةِ وَدَقَّ الْأَرْضَ بِرِجْلَيْهِ فَعَلاَ الْغُبَارُ وَارْتَفَعَ وَثَارَوَأَمَّا الْفَرَسُ فَإِنَّهُ شَخَرَ وَنَخَرَ وَصَهَلَ وَازْمَهَرَّ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala warāʾahu fī tilka al-ghābati fa-shaqqa al-jawādu fī wasaṭi al-ghābati wa-daqqa al-arḍa bi-rijlayhi fa-ʿalā al-ghubāru wa-irtafaʿa wa-thāra wa-ammā al-farasu fa-innahu shakhara wa-nakhara wa-ṣahala wa-izmaharra
sentences.l: So-he-entered behind-it into that the-wood; and-cleft the-steed into (the) middle (of) the-wood and-pounded the-ground with-its-two-legs, so-rose-high the-dust and-went-up and-flew-up. And-as-for the-horse, then-indeed-it snorted and-snored and-neighed and-glared.
sentences.i: So he followed it into that wood, and the steed tore its way into the heart of the wood, pounding the ground with its hooves, so that the dust rose and mounted and swirled up; and as for the horse, it snorted and blew and neighed and glared in fury.
sentences.n: The print has وراءة, a misprint for وراءه, corrected here. shaqqa fī, “to cleave (a way) into”: the horse breaks through the thicket. bi-rijlayhi, “with its two legs”: bi- marks the instrument; the dual is loose, for a horse's feet. The dust rises in three verbs, ʿalā, irtafaʿa, thāra, all with al-ghubāru as their subject. The print points فعَلاَ itself, with a fatḥa on the ʿayn and one set over the lām-alif, on the alif; both are kept. The print runs thāra and wa-ammā together as one word, وثاروامّا; it is kept as set and read as the two words wa-thāra wa-ammā. wa-ammā … fa-innahu, “and as for …, (then) it”: ammā is always answered by fa-; al-faras is often feminine, but here it takes the masculine -hu. The four verbs of the horse make rhymed pairs, shakhara / nakhara and ṣahala / izmaharra: shakhara and nakhara are “to snort, blow through the nostrils”; izmaharra, from the four-letter root z-m-h-r, is said of eyes reddening and a face glowering in anger. The ء of وراءه and the shaddas of فشقّ, ودقّ, وامّا and وازمهرّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ فِي تِلْكَ الْغَابَةِ أَسَدٌ عَظِيمُ الْخَطَرِ قَبِيحُ الْمَنْظَرِ عُيُونُهُ تَرْمِي بِالشَّرَرِ لَهُ وَجْهٌ عَبُوسٌ وَشَكْلٌ يَهُولُ النُّفُوسَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna fī tilka al-ghābati asadun ʿaẓīmu al-khaṭari qabīḥu al-manẓari ʿuyūnuhu tarmī bi-al-sharari lahu wajhun ʿabūsun wa-shaklun yahūlu al-nufūsa
sentences.l: And-there-was in that the-wood a-lion great (of) the-danger, ugly (of) the-look; its-eyes throw with-the-sparks; to-it (is) a-face frowning and-a-form (that) terrifies the-souls.
sentences.i: Now in that wood there was a lion, fearsome and foul to look upon, its eyes shooting sparks, with a scowling face and a shape to strike terror into the heart.
sentences.n: A description in rhymed prose: al-khaṭari / al-manẓari / bi-al-sharari, then ʿabūsun / al-nufūsa. wa-kāna fī tilka al-ghābati asadun, “and there was in that wood a lion”: the indefinite subject follows the phrase of place. ʿaẓīmu al-khaṭari and qabīḥu al-manẓari are adjectives in construct with a definite noun, “great of danger, ugly of aspect”, and stay indefinite in sense, agreeing with asadun. ʿuyūnuhu, “its eyes”, a plural for the pair, as often. tarmī bi-al-sharari, “throw out sparks”: ramā bi-, “to throw”, with bi- marking what is thrown; the phrase recalls the Qurʾān's picture of Hell (77:32). lahu wajhun, “to it (is) a face”: li- of possession. yahūlu, “terrifies”, from hāla, a hollow verb.

sentences.t: فَالْتَفَتَ الْخَازِنْدَارُ فَرَأَى ذٰلِكَ الْأَسَدَ قَاصِدًا إِلَيْهِ فَلَمْ يَجِدْ لَهُ مَهْرَبًا مِنْ يَدَيْهِ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ مَعَهُ سَيْفٌ
sentences.tr: fa-iltafata al-khāzindāru fa-raʾā dhālika al-asada qāṣidan ilayhi fa-lam yajid lahu mahraban min yadayhi wa-lam yakun maʿahu sayfun
sentences.l: So-turned the-treasurer and-saw that the-lion heading toward-him, and-not did-he-find for-himself a-place-of-flight from its-two-hands; and-not was with-him a-sword.
sentences.i: The treasurer turned and saw the lion making straight for him, and he could find no way of escape from its clutches; nor had he a sword with him.
sentences.n: qāṣidan ilayhi, “making for him”, an accusative of state: qaṣada, “to head for”, takes its goal directly or, as here, with ilā. lam yajid, “he did not find”, the jussive after lam. mahrab, “a place or means of flight”, from haraba, “to flee”; min yadayhi, “from its two hands”, that is, its paws, its grip. He had thrown his sword down when the horse bolted, the night before. The أ of فرأى is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللّٰهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla fī nafsihi lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīmi
sentences.l: So-he-said in himself: No power and-no strength except through-God, the-High, the-Mighty.
sentences.i: And he said within himself: There is no power and no strength save in God, the Most High, the Almighty.
sentences.n: fī nafsihi, “in himself”, to himself, unspoken. lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-Allāhi is the set formula of dismay and resignation: lā of absolute denial takes its noun in the accusative without tanwīn, and bi- means “in, through God”. The print runs each lā into its noun, لاحول and ولاقوة; they are kept as set and read as separate words.

sentences.t: مَاحَصَلَ لِي هٰذَا الضِّيقُ إِلَّا بِذَنْبِ الْأَمْجَدِ وَالْأَسْعَدِ وَإِنَّ هٰذِهِ السَّفْرَةَ مَشُوُمَةٌ مِنْ أَوَّلِهَا
sentences.tr: mā ḥaṣala lī hādhā al-ḍīqu illā bi-dhanbi al-Amjadi wa-al-Asʿadi wa-inna hādhihi al-safrata mashūmatun min awwalihā
sentences.l: Not befell to-me this the-distress except by-(the)-sin (of) al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad; and-indeed this the-journey (is) ill-omened from its-first.
sentences.i: This strait has come upon me only for the wrong done to al-Amjad and al-Asʿad; this journey has been ill-starred from the very first.
sentences.n: The print runs mā and ḥaṣala together, ماحصل; it is kept as set. mā … illā, “nothing … but”, restricts the cause: “only through”. bi-dhanbi, “by the sin of”: bi- of cause; dhanb al-Amjadi wa-al-Asʿadi is the wrong done to them, the sin of putting them to death, not a sin of theirs. ḍīq, “straitness, distress”. safra, “journey”. The print sets a ḍamma on the wāw of مشوُمة, kept here; the word is mashʾūma, “ill-omened”, written without its hamza and said mashūma. The shaddas of الّا and اوّلها are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْأَمْجَدَ وَالْأَسْعَدَ قَدْ حَمِيَ عَلَيْهِمَا الْحَرُّ فَعَطِشَا عَطَشًا شَدِيدًا حَتَّى نَزَلَتْ أَلْسِنَتُهُمَا وَاسْتَغَاثَا مِنَ الْعَطَشِ فَلَمْ يُغِثْهُمَا أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-Amjada wa-al-Asʿada qad ḥamiya ʿalayhimā al-ḥarru fa-ʿaṭishā ʿaṭashan shadīdan ḥattā nazalat alsinatuhumā wa-istaghāthā mina al-ʿaṭashi fa-lam yughithhumā aḥadun
sentences.l: Then indeed al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad — had grown-hot upon-them-two the-heat, so-they-two-thirsted a-thirst intense, until hung-down their-two-tongues; and-they-two-cried-for-help from the-thirst, and-not helped-them-two anyone.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the heat had beaten down on al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, and they grew so terribly thirsty that their tongues hung from their mouths; they cried out for help in their thirst, but no one came to help them.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it is so) that”, turns the story back to the brothers, a common hinge of the storyteller's style; inna puts them first as a topic, and the clause about them follows. ḥamiya ʿalayhimā al-ḥarru, “the heat grew hot upon them”. ʿaṭashan shadīdan, “a severe thirst”, the verbal noun of the verb itself as its object, to strengthen it. nazalat alsinatuhumā, “their tongues came down”, lolled out: alsina, plural of lisān, for the two brothers' tongues; the verb is feminine before a broken plural. istaghāthā, Form X of gh-w-th, “to call for help”; lam yughithhumā, Form IV aghātha, “to come to the help of”, jussive after lam. The shadda of الحرّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَا يَالَيْتَنَا كُنَّا قُتِلْنَا وَاسْتَرَحْنَا مِنْ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālā yā laytanā kunnā qutilnā wa-istaraḥnā min hādhā
sentences.l: So-they-two-said: O would-that-we had-been we-were-killed and-we-were-at-rest from this!
sentences.i: And they said: Would that we had been killed and had found rest from this!
sentences.n: The print runs yā and laytanā together, ياليتنا; it is kept as set. yā laytanā, “O would that we”: layta takes its noun as a suffix, -nā, and yā here only strengthens the wish. kunnā qutilnā, “we had been killed”: kāna with a perfect sets the wish in the past. istaraḥnā, Form X of r-w-ḥ, “to find rest, be relieved”; min marks what one is relieved of. The shadda of كنّا and the ḍamma of قُتلنا are printed.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ مَا نَدْرِي أَيْنَ جَفَلَ الْحِصَانُ حَتَّى ذَهَبَ الْخَازِنْدَارُ وَرَاءَهُ وَخَلَّانَا مُكَتَّفِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin mā nadrī ayna jafala al-ḥiṣānu ḥattā dhahaba al-khāzindāru warāʾahu wa-khallānā mukattafīna
sentences.l: But not we-know where bolted the-horse, so-that went the-treasurer behind-it and-left-us bound.
sentences.i: But we do not know where the horse has bolted to, so that the treasurer has gone after it and left us here bound.
sentences.n: The print has وراءة, a misprint for وراءه, corrected here. mā nadrī, “we do not know”, mā negating the imperfect, as in the everyday language. ḥattā with the perfect, “so that”, of what actually followed. khallā, Form II of kh-l-w, “to leave, let be”, a verb of the spoken language; -nā is its object. mukattafīna, “bound, with arms tied”, passive participle of Form II kattafa, an accusative of state; it is plural where the two brothers would take the dual, a habit of the later language. The ء of وراءه and the shaddas of وخلّانا and مكتّفين are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَوْ جَاءَنَا وَقَتَلَنَا كَانَ أَرْيَحَ لَنَا مِنْ مُقَاسَاةِ هٰذَا الْعَذَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-law jāʾanā wa-qatalanā kāna aryaḥa lanā min muqāsāti hādhā al-ʿadhābi
sentences.l: So-if he-had-come-to-us and-killed-us, it-would-have-been more-restful for-us than (the) enduring (of) this the-torment.
sentences.i: Had he come back and killed us, it would have been easier for us than to endure this torment.
sentences.n: law, “if (it had been so)”, of an unreal condition; its answer, kāna, stands without the la- that Classical usually puts before it. aryaḥ, “more restful, easier”, an elative formed on the spoken stem rayyaḥ, where Classical has arwaḥ (from r-w-ḥ); it is the predicate of kāna, hence the accusative. min after the elative, “than”. muqāsāt, verbal noun of Form III qāsā, “to suffer, endure”. The ء of جاءنا and the fatḥas of وقتَلَنا are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَسْعَدُ يَا أَخِي اصْبِرْ فَسَوْفَ يَأْتِينَا فَرَجُ اللّٰهِ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Asʿadu yā akhī iṣbir fa-sawfa yaʾtīnā faraju Allāhi subḥānahu wa-taʿālā
sentences.l: So-said al-Asʿad: O my-brother, be-patient, for-will come-to-us (the) relief (of) God, glory-to-Him and-exalted-is-He.
sentences.i: Al-Asʿad said: My brother, be patient; the deliverance of God, glory be to Him, the Exalted, will surely come to us.
sentences.n: iṣbir, imperative of ṣabara, “to be patient”. fa-sawfa, “for (it) will”: sawfa marks the future. faraj, “relief, release from trouble”. subḥānahu wa-taʿālā, “glory be to Him, and exalted is He”, the praise added after the name of God. The أ of أخي and of يأتينا is printed.

sentences.t: كَأَنَّ الْحِصَانَ مَا جَفَلَ إِلَّا لِأَجْلِ لُطْفِ اللّٰهِ بِنَا وَمَا ضَرَّنَا غَيْرُ هٰذَا الْعَطَشِ
sentences.tr: ka-anna al-ḥiṣāna mā jafala illā li-ajli luṭfi Allāhi binā wa-mā ḍarranā ghayru hādhā al-ʿaṭashi
sentences.l: As-if the-horse not bolted except for-(the)-sake (of the) kindness (of) God to-us; and-not harmed-us other-than this the-thirst.
sentences.i: It is as though the horse bolted only because God was being kind to us, and nothing has harmed us but this thirst.
sentences.n: كان is read ka-anna, “as if”, written, as the print writes hamza, with bare alif; ka-anna takes its noun, al-ḥiṣāna, in the accusative. It could also be kāna, used loosely at the head of the clause as the spoken language does, with much the same sense; al-ḥiṣān would then be nominative, al-ḥiṣānu. mā … illā li-ajli, “only for the sake of”: li-ajli, “for the sake of, because of”. luṭf, “kindness, gracious care”, of God's hidden mercy; bi- marks the ones it is shown to. ghayru, “other than”, is the subject of ḍarra, hence the nominative. The shaddas of الّا and ضرّنا are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ هَزَّ نَفْسَهُ وَتَحَرَّكَ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَانْحَلَّ كِتَافُهُ فَقَامَ وَحَلَّ كِتَافَ أَخِيهِ ثُمَّ أَخَذَ سَيْفَ الْأَمِيرِ
sentences.tr: thumma hazza nafsahu wa-taḥarraka yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-inḥalla kitāfuhu fa-qāma wa-ḥalla kitāfa akhīhi thumma akhadha sayfa al-amīri
sentences.l: Then he-shook himself and-moved right and-left, so-came-loose his-bond; so-he-rose and-untied (the) bond (of) his-brother; then he-took (the) sword (of) the-emir.
sentences.i: Then he shook himself and twisted to the right and to the left until his bonds came loose; he got up and untied his brother's bonds, and then took up the emir's sword.
sentences.n: hazza nafsahu, “he shook himself”: nafs with a suffix serves as the reflexive. yamīnan wa-shimālan, “right and left”, accusatives of direction. inḥalla, Form VII of ḥ-l-l, “to come undone”, the passive-like partner of ḥalla, “to untie”, which follows at once. kitāf, the cord that ties a captive's arms behind him. al-amīr, “the emir”, is the treasurer, a man of rank; this is the sword he threw down when he ran after his horse. The shaddas of هزّ, وتحرّك, فانحلّ and وحلّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِأَخِيهِ وَاللّٰهِ لَانَرُوحُ مِنْ هَا هُنَا حَتَّى نَكْشِفَ خَبَرَهُ وَنَعْرِفَ مَاجَرَى لَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla li-akhīhi wa-Allāhi lā narūḥu min hā hunā ḥattā nakshifa khabarahu wa-naʿrifa mā jarā lahu
sentences.l: And-he-said to-his-brother: By-God, not we-go from here until we-uncover his-news and-we-know what happened to-him.
sentences.i: And he said to his brother: By God, we will not leave this place until we have found out what has become of him and know what has befallen him.
sentences.n: The print has خبرة, a misprint for خبره, corrected here. wa-Allāhi, “by God”: the wāw of oath, with the genitive. The print runs lā and narūḥu together, لانروح, and mā and jarā, ماجرى; both are kept as set. rāḥa, “to go”, a verb of the spoken language. hā hunā, “here”, with the presentative hā, printed apart. ḥattā with the subjunctive, nakshifa … wa-naʿrifa, “until we uncover … and know”, of something still to come. kashafa khabarahu, “to uncover his news”, to find out what happened to him. jarā li-, “to happen to”.

sentences.t: وَشَرَعَا يَقْتَصَّانِ الْأَثَرَ فَدَلَّهُمَا عَلَى الْغَابَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-sharaʿā yaqtaṣṣāni al-athara fa-dallahumā ʿalā al-ghābati
sentences.l: And-they-two-began they-two-follow the-track, and-it-guided-them-two to the-wood.
sentences.i: So they set about following the tracks, and the trail led them to the wood.
sentences.n: sharaʿa with an imperfect, “to set about doing”, marks the start of an action. iqtaṣṣa al-athara, Form VIII of q-ṣ-ṣ, “to follow the track”, step by step. dalla ʿalā, “to guide to, point the way to”: ʿalā marks the goal; its subject is the track. The shaddas of يقتصّان and فدلّهما are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَا لِبَعْضِهِمَا إِنَّ الْحِصَانَ وَالْخَازِنْدَارَ مَا تَجَاوَزَا هٰذِهِ الْغَابَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālā li-baʿḍihimā inna al-ḥiṣāna wa-al-khāzindāra mā tajāwazā hādhihi al-ghābata
sentences.l: So-they-two-said to-each-other-of-them-two: Indeed the-horse and-the-treasurer not passed-beyond this the-wood.
sentences.i: And they said to each other: The horse and the treasurer have not gone past this wood.
sentences.n: li-baʿḍihimā, “to some of them two”, is “to each other”, a usage of the later language. tajāwazā, Form VI of j-w-z, “to pass beyond”, dual, for the horse and the treasurer together.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَسْعَدُ لِأَخِيهِ قِفْ هُنَا حَتَّى أَدْخُلَ الْغَابَةَ وَأَنْظُرَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Asʿadu li-akhīhi qif hunā ḥattā adkhula al-ghābata wa-anẓurahā
sentences.l: So-said al-Asʿad to-his-brother: Stand here until I-enter the-wood and-look-it-over.
sentences.i: Al-Asʿad said to his brother: Wait here while I go into the wood and look it over.
sentences.n: qif, imperative of waqafa, “to stand, stop”, which loses its first radical. ḥattā with the subjunctive, “until, so that I may”. naẓara takes the wood directly, anẓurahā, “look it over”, where Classical prefers naẓara ilā or fī.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْأَمْجَدُ مَا أُخَلِّيكَ تَدْخُلُ فِيهَا وَحْدَكَ وَمَا نَدْخُلُ إِلَّا جَمِيعًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-Amjadu mā ukhallīka tadkhulu fīhā waḥdaka wa-mā nadkhulu illā jamīʿan
sentences.l: So-said to-him al-Amjad: Not I-let-you you-enter into-it alone-you, and-not we-enter except all-together.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said to him: I will not let you go into it alone; we go in together or not at all.
sentences.n: mā ukhallīka tadkhulu, “I will not let you go in”: khallā, “to let”, takes its object and then a bare imperfect, the way the spoken language says it. waḥdaka, “by yourself”, an accusative with the suffix. mā … illā jamīʿan, “not … except all together”.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ سَلِمْنَا سَلِمْنَا سَوَاءً وَإِنْ عَطِبْنَا عَطِبْنَا سَوَاءً
sentences.tr: fa-in salimnā salimnā sawāʾan wa-in ʿaṭibnā ʿaṭibnā sawāʾan
sentences.l: So-if we-are-safe, we-are-safe alike; and-if we-perish, we-perish alike.
sentences.i: If we come through, we come through together, and if we perish, we perish together.
sentences.n: Two matched conditions, each verb repeated in its own answer: in with the perfect, of a possible future. salima, “to be safe”, and ʿaṭiba, “to perish”, are the usual pair. sawāʾan, “equally, together”, an accusative used adverbially.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَ الِاثْنَانِ فَوَجَدَا الْأَسَدَ قَدْ هَجَمَ عَلَى الْخَازِنْدَارِ وَهُوَ تَحْتَهُ كَأَنَّهُ عُصْفُورٌ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhala al-ithnāni fa-wajadā al-asada qad hajama ʿalā al-khāzindāri wa-huwa taḥtahu ka-annahu ʿuṣfūrun
sentences.l: So-entered the-two, and-they-two-found the-lion had fallen upon the-treasurer, and-he (was) beneath-it as-if-he (were) a-sparrow.
sentences.i: So the two of them went in, and found that the lion had sprung upon the treasurer, who lay beneath it like a sparrow.
sentences.n: dakhala al-ithnāni: the verb stands before its dual subject in the singular; the next verb, wajadā, coming after it, is dual. qad hajama, “had fallen upon”: wajada with a clause, “found that it had”. wa-huwa taḥtahu, “and he beneath it”, a circumstantial clause. ka-annahu ʿuṣfūrun, “as though he were a sparrow”: ka-anna takes its noun as the suffix -hu, its predicate in the nominative.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنَّهُ صَارَ يَبْتَهِلُ إِلَى اللّٰهِ وَيُشِيرُ إِلَيْهِ نَحْوَ السَّمَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākinnahu ṣāra yabtahilu ilā Allāhi wa-yushīru ilayhi naḥwa al-samāʾi
sentences.l: But-he began he-implores to God and-he-points to-Him toward the-sky.
sentences.i: Yet he was calling humbly upon God and pointing up to Him toward the sky.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “he set to doing, was doing”, in the spoken use of the verb. ibtahala ilā, Form VIII of b-h-l, “to pray humbly to”. ashāra ilā, Form IV of sh-w-r, “to point at, make a sign to”; naḥwa, “toward”. The ء of السماء is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُ الْأَمْجَدُ أَخَذَ السَّيْفَ وَهَجَمَ عَلَى الْأَسَدِ وَضَرَبَهُ بِالسَّيْفِ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ فَقَتَلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu al-Amjadu akhadha al-sayfa wa-hajama ʿalā al-asadi wa-ḍarabahu bi-al-sayfi bayna ʿaynayhi fa-qatalahu
sentences.l: And-when saw-him al-Amjad, he-took the-sword and-rushed upon the-lion and-struck-it with-the-sword between its-two-eyes and-killed-it.
sentences.i: When al-Amjad saw him, he took the sword, rushed upon the lion and struck it between the eyes, and killed it.
sentences.n: hajama ʿalā, “to rush upon, attack”: ʿalā marks the one attacked. bi-al-sayfi: bi- marks the instrument. The آ of رآه and the أ of الأسد are printed.

sentences.t: وَوَقَعَ الْأَسَدُ مَطْرُوحًا عَلَى الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: wa-waqaʿa al-asadu maṭrūḥan ʿalā al-arḍi
sentences.l: And-fell the-lion cast-down on the-ground.
sentences.i: And the lion fell and lay stretched upon the ground.
sentences.n: maṭrūḥan, “thrown down”, passive participle of ṭaraḥa, an accusative of state.

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَ الْأَمِيرُ وَهُوَ مُتَعَجِّبٌ مِنْ هٰذَا الْأَمْرِ فَرَأَى الْأَمْجَدَ وَالْأَسْعَدَ وَلَدَيْ سَيِّدِهِ وَاقِفَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍa al-amīru wa-huwa mutaʿajjibun min hādhā al-amri fa-raʾā al-Amjada wa-al-Asʿada waladay sayyidihi wāqifayni
sentences.l: So-rose the-emir, and-he (was) wondering at this the-matter, and-he-saw al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad, (the) two-sons (of) his-master, standing.
sentences.i: The emir got to his feet, astonished at what had happened, and saw al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, his master's two sons, standing there.
sentences.n: The print has سيدة, a misprint for سيده, corrected here: waladay sayyidihi, “the two sons of his master”, the king. wa-huwa mutaʿajjibun, “he being astonished”, a circumstantial clause; mutaʿajjib, Form V participle of ʿ-j-b. waladay, dual of walad in construct, which drops its nūn, in the accusative in apposition to the two names. wāqifayni, “standing”, dual, an accusative of state; the print's واقفين could equally be the plural wāqifīna, the later language's habit with two. The أ of فرأى and the shadda of متعجّب are printed.

sentences.t: فَتَرَامَى عَلَى أَقْدَامِهِمَا وَقَالَ لَهُمَا وَاللّٰهِ يَا سَيِّدَايَ مَا يَصْلُحُ أَنْ أُفَرِّطَ فِيكُمَا بِقَتْلِكُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-tarāmā ʿalā aqdāmihimā wa-qāla lahumā wa-Allāhi yā sayyidāya mā yaṣluḥu an ufarriṭa fīkumā bi-qatlikumā
sentences.l: So-he-threw-himself upon their-two-feet and-said to-them-two: By-God, O my-two-masters, not it-is-fitting that I-squander you-two by-killing-you-two.
sentences.i: He threw himself at their feet and said to them: By God, my lords, it is not right that I should throw your lives away by killing you.
sentences.n: tarāmā ʿalā, Form VI of r-m-y, “to throw oneself upon”. aqdām, plural of qadam, “foot”, for the feet of the two. yā sayyidāya, “O my two masters”: the dual keeps its nominative form sayyidā before the suffix, where Classical would have the oblique sayyidayya. farraṭa fī, Form II of f-r-ṭ, “to neglect, let go to waste”: fī marks what is squandered. bi-qatlikumā: bi- of means, “by killing you”.

sentences.t: فَلَا كَانَ مَنْ يَقْتُلُكُمَا فَبِرُوحِي أَفْدِيكُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-lā kāna man yaqtulukumā fa-bi-rūḥī afdīkumā
sentences.l: So-may-not be (he) who kills-you-two; for-with-my-soul I-ransom-you-two.
sentences.i: Perish the man who would kill you! I would give my own life for yours.
sentences.n: fa-lā kāna man, “may there not be one who”: lā with the perfect makes a wish, here a curse. fadā X bi-Y, “to ransom X with Y”: bi- marks what is given in exchange, his own soul; the phrase is set first for weight. afdī, imperfect of fadā.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahr Zāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The print sets the name as two words, شهر زاد; it is kept so. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
